title: Pearson VUE recall 33
des: DOH (HAAD) paediatrics recall, Pearson VUE paper 33

questions.question: A child after a road traffic accident has signs of raised intracranial pressure: HR 72, unequal pupils and high blood pressure. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Bradycardia, hypertension and unequal pupils (Cushing response with herniation) need immediate ICP-lowering therapy (3% saline 3–5 mL/kg or mannitol, head up 30°, normocapnia) before transfer to CT. Never treat the hypertension: it maintains cerebral perfusion.

questions.question: A child has blunt abdominal trauma during sport, with periumbilical pain. He is conscious and haemodynamically stable. What is the best investigation?
questions.exp: In a stable child with significant blunt abdominal trauma, contrast CT shows solid organ, bowel and pancreatic injury. Unstable children go to theatre; FAST is adjunctive only.

questions.question: A child is bitten on the index finger by a venomous snake and has local swelling and systemic signs. What is the specific management?
questions.exp: Immobilise the limb, give supportive care and antivenom for systemic envenomation or progressive local swelling. Tourniquets, incision and suction are harmful.

questions.question: A child with head injury after an RTA is unstable and remains hypotensive after 40 mL/kg of crystalloid. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Hypotension after trauma is haemorrhage until proved otherwise. After 40 mL/kg of crystalloid, give blood (10–20 mL/kg packed red cells, major haemorrhage protocol) and look for the bleeding source; inotropes are not first-line in haemorrhagic shock. (The recall's options did not include blood; it was added.)

questions.question: A child rescued from a fire has no burns but has smoke inhalation, is intubated and has severe metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Enclosed-space fires release CO and hydrogen cyanide, both cause tissue hypoxia and lactic acidosis. Give 100% oxygen; consider hydroxocobalamin if lactate is very high. Pulse oximetry is falsely normal in CO poisoning; check co-oximetry.

questions.question: A child has recurrent otitis media and sinusitis. His brother has cystic fibrosis. Sweat chloride is 40 mmol/L on two occasions; he is otherwise well. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Sweat chloride 30–59 mmol/L is intermediate. Next step is extended CFTR mutation analysis; if inconclusive, CFTR function tests (nasal potential difference or intestinal current measurement). IRT is a newborn screening test only.
questions.c: CFTR genetic analysis (extended), then nasal potential difference if unclear

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis has repeated chest infections and now epigastric pain radiating to the back. What is the best investigation?
questions.exp: Acute pancreatitis can occur in CF, especially in pancreatic-sufficient patients. Raised amylase and lipase (>3× normal) with epigastric pain radiating to the back confirms it.

questions.question: A girl has recurrent syncope and congenital sensorineural deafness. ECG shows long QT. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen: autosomal recessive long QT (KCNQ1/KCNE1) with congenital deafness. Romano–Ward is autosomal dominant LQT without deafness.

questions.question: Which ECG finding is normal in a 3-week-old neonate?
questions.exp: Normal neonatal ECG: right axis (up to +180°), dominant R in V1, and T waves in V1 that become INVERTED after day 3–7. An upright T in V1 after the first week suggests right ventricular hypertrophy; inverted P in lead II suggests an ectopic rhythm or dextrocardia. (Options reconstructed.)
questions.a: Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1
questions.c: Inverted P wave in lead II

questions.question: A child has fever, convulsions and a focal deficit. CT shows a ring-enhancing lesion. What is the underlying predisposing condition?
questions.exp: Brain abscess in children is associated with cyanotic CHD (right-to-left shunt bypasses the lung filter), as well as sinusitis, otitis and mastoiditis.

questions.question: A 1-year-old has recurrent episodes of crying then turning blue, going limp and falling, with full recovery. Examination is normal. What is the most useful investigation?
questions.exp: Breath-holding spells are benign but are linked with iron deficiency; iron treatment reduces their frequency even without anaemia. Do an ECG if spells are atypical (no trigger) to exclude long QT. EEG is not needed. (Two recalled questions merged.)
questions.a: Full blood count and iron studies

questions.question: A girl has short stature. What is the most important investigation?
questions.exp: Every girl with unexplained short stature should have a karyotype to exclude Turner syndrome, which may have no other obvious features.

questions.question: A girl has precocious puberty, large irregular café-au-lait patches and hyperthyroidism. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: McCune–Albright (GNAS mosaic activating mutation): polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, 'coast of Maine' café-au-lait macules and autonomous endocrine overactivity (peripheral precocious puberty, hyperthyroidism, GH excess, Cushing).

questions.question: A boy has pubic hair and adult body odour, but his testes are small (prepubertal). What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Virilisation with prepubertal testes = peripheral (gonadotrophin-independent) precocity from the adrenal: non-classic CAH or an adrenal tumour. Central puberty would enlarge the testes.

questions.question: A teenager has high blood pressure with attacks of sweating, flushing and headache. What is the best test?
questions.exp: Paroxysmal hypertension with sweating, palpitations and headache suggests phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma. Measure plasma free or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines, then image.

questions.question: A child has high blood pressure on two separate occasions. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Confirm sustained hypertension with ABPM before work-up and treatment; lifestyle advice in the meantime.

questions.question: A girl has generalised proximal muscle weakness (power 4/5) without ptosis or skin changes, and cannot do her usual activities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Slowly progressive proximal weakness of shoulder and pelvic girdles with normal eyes and skin suggests limb-girdle dystrophy. Myasthenia usually involves ptosis/diplopia and fatigability; dermatomyositis has the heliotrope rash and Gottron papules.

questions.question: A child has abdominal pain, arthritis and a purpuric rash on the legs. Which investigation supports the diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (HSP): platelets are normal; serum IgA is raised in about half and skin/renal biopsy shows IgA deposition. Low complement suggests post-streptococcal GN or SLE; schistocytes suggest HUS.
questions.a: Raised serum IgA (IgA deposits on biopsy)

questions.question: An infant has 3 days of high fever; as the fever settles, a pink maculopapular rash appears on the trunk. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum) is caused by HHV-6 (and HHV-7). It can cause febrile convulsions. Parvovirus gives slapped cheek; coxsackie hand, foot and mouth disease.

questions.question: A child has recurrent skin and organ abscesses with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: CGD: recurrent catalase-positive abscesses (skin, liver, lymph nodes), granulomas, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Granulomas can produce calcitriol, which explains hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria in the original scenario. Diagnose with DHR test.

questions.question: An infant has chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive and generalised lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chronic diarrhoea, FTT, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, oral thrush and recurrent infections in an infant should prompt HIV testing (PCR under 18 months).

questions.question: A preterm baby has a cranial ultrasound showing haemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix without intraventricular extension. What grade is this?
questions.exp: Papile grading: I germinal matrix only, II intraventricular blood without dilatation, III with ventricular dilatation, IV periventricular haemorrhagic infarction. (Stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: A child born very preterm with a long NICU stay has spastic diplegia. What is the expected MRI finding?
questions.exp: PVL (white matter injury around the lateral ventricles) affects descending fibres to the legs, giving spastic diplegia. Basal ganglia/thalamic injury follows acute profound hypoxia in term babies (dyskinetic CP).

questions.question: What is part of the management of chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia)?
questions.exp: BPD: optimise nutrition, target oxygen saturations, diuretics (furosemide, thiazides) for fluid-related deterioration, bronchodilators in selected cases, and low-dose dexamethasone (DART) only to aid extubation. Fluid restriction, not fluid loading.

questions.question: A previously well 15-year-old girl spends most of the time in her room, does not join family activities and says 'it's not your business', but her school performance is good. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.exp: Seeking privacy and independence with preserved school performance, friendships, sleep and appetite is normal adolescence. A fall in grades, withdrawal from friends, sleep or appetite change would suggest depression; use the HEADSSS interview.

questions.question: A toddler has abnormal behaviour and delayed speech, and autism is suspected. What is the first assessment?
questions.exp: Formal audiology (and vision) must be done early in any child with language delay or suspected ASD, because hearing loss can mimic or coexist with autism.

questions.question: A child has a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria). What is the most important diagnosis to exclude?
questions.exp: Leukocoria needs urgent ophthalmology referral to exclude retinoblastoma, which is life-threatening. Cataract is commoner but the priority is to exclude the tumour.

questions.question: Newborn screening shows raised galactose-1-phosphate (galactosaemia). What is the initial action?
questions.exp: Classic galactosaemia (GALT deficiency): stop all lactose (breast milk and cow's milk formula) immediately and start soy or lactose-free formula; watch for E. coli sepsis, jaundice and cataracts.
questions.a: Stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula
questions.b: Stop breastfeeding and start cow's milk formula

questions.question: A neonate has deranged liver function, coagulopathy and suspected tyrosinaemia type 1. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Succinylacetone in urine or blood is pathognomonic for tyrosinaemia type 1 (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency). Tyrosine is raised in many liver diseases. Treat with nitisinone (NTBC) and a low-tyrosine/phenylalanine diet.

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis on treatment cannot walk and has bone manifestations. Which vitamin deficiency is responsible?
questions.exp: Pancreatic insufficiency causes fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (A, D, E, K). Vitamin D deficiency gives rickets/osteomalacia with bone pain and difficulty walking. Vitamin E deficiency gives ataxia and neuropathy.

questions.question: A child has chronic diarrhoea and dermatitis around the mouth and nappy area. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.exp: Acrodermatitis enteropathica (inherited SLC39A4 or acquired zinc deficiency): periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhoea and alopecia. Responds dramatically to zinc.

questions.question: A child has niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency. Which features are expected?
questions.exp: Pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis (Casal necklace), diarrhoea and dementia (and death). Seen in Hartnup disease and carcinoid. Thiamine deficiency = Wernicke; vitamin C = scurvy; vitamin A = night blindness.

questions.question: A child has deranged liver function. The mother tells you privately that she thinks her daughter has been taking a drug. Which drug is most likely?
questions.exp: Paracetamol overdose is the commonest intentional overdose in adolescents and causes hepatotoxicity. Check a timed level, treat with N-acetylcysteine and arrange a psychosocial assessment.

questions.question: A girl is booked for tonsillectomy. Pre-operative tests show a prolonged APTT (120 s) with normal PT and no bleeding history. Which factor deficiency is expected?
questions.exp: A very prolonged APTT without any bleeding history is typical of factor XII deficiency (or lupus anticoagulant). It does not cause bleeding, so surgery can go ahead. Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT.

questions.question: A child with leukaemia starting chemotherapy develops tumour lysis syndrome. Which laboratory finding is NOT expected?
questions.exp: TLS: hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and secondary hypocalcaemia (calcium binds phosphate), with acute kidney injury. Hypophosphataemia is not a feature. (Options reconstructed.)

questions.question: A teenager has died after unsuccessful CPR in hospital. The parents were not there. How should you break the news?
questions.exp: Breaking bad news (SPIKES): quiet private setting, senior clinician, find out what they know, give a warning shot ('I'm afraid I have bad news'), use clear words ('died'), allow silence and emotions, and offer support.
questions.a: Take them to a private room, introduce yourself, give a warning shot and then tell them clearly
questions.b: Ask them to calm down before speaking
questions.c: Tell them in the corridor straight away
questions.d: Ask the nurse to tell them

questions.question: A paediatric registrar has many complex duties and feels emotionally exhausted and detached. What is the main concern about burnout?
questions.exp: Burnout (emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, low accomplishment) is linked to medical errors, poor professionalism and lower patient satisfaction; it needs support and system change.
questions.a: It affects professional behaviour and patient safety
questions.b: It is a personal matter with no effect on practice
questions.c: It only matters if it causes physical illness
questions.d: It improves with taking on more work

questions.question: A researcher studies a new IV fluid. All children receiving IV fluids in the hospital are followed to see who received saline and who received the new fluid, and their outcomes are compared. What type of study is this?
questions.exp: Participants are grouped by exposure (which fluid they received, not allocated by the researcher) and followed for outcomes: an observational cohort study. In an RCT the investigator randomises the exposure; a case-control study starts from the outcome.

questions.question: A child has an acute limp after a viral illness, is afebrile and well, with mildly reduced hip movement and normal inflammatory markers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Transient synovitis: age 3–8, after a viral illness, afebrile, can weight-bear. Kocher criteria (fever, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12) point to septic arthritis. Settles in 1–2 weeks with rest and NSAIDs. (Stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: An active 13-year-old boy has pain and a tender swelling over the tibial tuberosity, worse with running and kneeling. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Osgood–Schlatter is traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity in active adolescents. Sinding-Larsen–Johansson affects the inferior pole of the patella. Manage with rest, ice, analgesia and stretching. (Stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: A child has fever and refuses to eat or drink. There are vesicles and ulcers on the soft palate and tonsillar pillars, with no gum involvement. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Herpangina (coxsackie A): ulcers at the back of the mouth (soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars). Herpetic gingivostomatitis gives anterior ulcers with swollen bleeding gums. Main risk is dehydration.

questions.question: A child with Kawasaki disease and an abnormal echocardiogram was treated with IVIG and aspirin. What advice do you give the mother on discharge?
questions.exp: IVIG antibodies block the response to live vaccines, so MMR and varicella are delayed 11 months. Children on long-term aspirin should get the inactivated influenza vaccine yearly (Reye syndrome risk), not the live nasal vaccine.
questions.a: Delay live vaccines (MMR, varicella) for 11 months after IVIG
questions.c: Give the live nasal influenza vaccine every year
questions.d: No change to the vaccine schedule
